utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've already met. My name is Rupert Elderkin. And as we go through this examination, I'd ask that we both try and keep our speaking speed slow enough for the interpreters to keep up with us, in particular since I know that you understand English very well, but, please, wait for the translation into your own language before you reply.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please say your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: My name is Meho Dzebo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: 13th of July, 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I was born in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I grew up in Zepa, my birth place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you, at some time, perform service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please tell us when was that, and in what function you served.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I served in Zagreb from April 1982 until May 1983. And I served the army as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you remain on the reserve after completing your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. I was deployed to the reserve station of the police in Rogatica and its department in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war started?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I'm a tool and die maker by profession, and I worked on maintaining machines at the Sjemec building timber factory in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And were you living as well in Rogatica before the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, I used to have a family house in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, going to the beginning of the war time period, were you ever mobilised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move on, I just want to know what is your citizenship, of which state in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the outbreak of the war, I was a citizen of Yugoslavia, and since the war, I have been a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Currently, I have dual citizenship. In addition to Bosnia-Herzegovina citizenship, I also have the United States citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, talking now about the period at the beginning of the 1990s, were you ever mobilised from the police reserve?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I was mobilised to the reserve police force on the 19th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did that mobilisation involve?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It means that I was activated to the police station where I had my war time deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: That was in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How long did that period of mobilisation last?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It lasted up until the beginning of the war, but I was withdrawn in January 1992, back to Rogatica, in order to man the composition of their unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: After being withdrawn back to Rogatica, did you return to Zepa at some point?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to Zepa on the 21st of July, 1992, after the fall of Rogatica, and after that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of that move from Rogatica to Zepa? Were you travelling on your own? Did you move with other people?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We travelled by groups. There would be groups of 20, 30, up to 50 people, and the people were withdrawing through the woods, to the free territories which existed at the time, and that was the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said that Rogatica was occupied. Again, to be clear for the record, occupied by whom?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska and the then-JNA occupied it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who were the people in the groups that were withdrawing to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: That was mostly the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When you went to Zepa, where did you go to live?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I went to my parents, and I spent the rest of the war in their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you give us a basic description of where your parents' house is in relation to the centre of Zepa town itself.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It is in a hamlet called Krnici [phoen], which is 4 kilometres to the north of the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was living in this house with you during the war time period?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: My parents, myself with my wife and our two children, and my younger brother with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you participate in the defence of Zepa after you arrived in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately in July 1992, when I arrived, I joined the army or the then-Territorial Defence of Zepa, actually. And I remained with them until the November of the same year. After that, I was transferred again to the reserve police station in Zepa, and I remained there until the end; that is to say, until the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there any reason for that transfer that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, probably as my war time assignment was a position in the reserve police station, that could have been the only reason for them to transfer me back there once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was your role on the police reserve when you transferred back to that, at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, until April 1993 -- from the moment of my return, until April 1993 [as interpreted], I had the duties of a regular policeman. And from April 1993, until July 1995, I worked at the crime prevention department of the police as an assistant -- an assistant to the inspectors who were working within this department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us briefly what that role with the crime prevention inspectors involved.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, as I was wounded, I was moving with difficulty, and I was mostly in charge of administrative duties, such as taking statements from citizens who had been brought in, making Official Notes, and that was it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you were wounded. Could you tell us the circumstances in which you sustained this wound?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: As we were leaving Rogatica after the occupation, I managed to activate a land-mine, a trip mine, when we were leaving the town, and these were the circumstances under which I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you based as a police officer specifically? I know it was in the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: At the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there a specific building that was the police building?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. It was the building of the agricultural co-operative, and in one room we were housed. And there was the Red Cross in another building on the same floor [as interpreted]. And on the floor above us was the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you perform any policing duties at any other location, apart from in this building in the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you wear a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We had no uniforms. We worked in our civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And were you armed?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Until the arrival of UNPROFOR in May 1993, we had weapons that belonged to the reserve police force. After that, in May 1993, we handed over our weapons to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were other men in the police or in the Bosnian Army armed even after UNPROFOR arrived, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: People had kept some side-arms, those who managed to keep something without handing it into UNPROFOR, but that was a very small quantity. And these were mainly pistols and hunting guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about weapons being brought into the enclave; for example, by way of helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was four or five helicopter flights by which weapons were delivered to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about the conditions in the Zepa enclave. Can you please describe, as best you can, what the living conditions were like throughout the war, if you go year by year? And I'm particularly interested to hear about the food situation, medical care, and safety and security for the population. So starting in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. 1992 and up until the arrival of the UNPROFOR, that is to say, up until May 1993, the situation was awful, beginning with the security situation and managing to obtain food and medication and all that. We got a lot of help from NATO aircraft during the time while they provided deliveries of food. After the arrival of UNPROFOR, there was quite enough food and medications. And the security was at a much higher and better level, excluding the last offensive and the fall of Zepa in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief account, then, of the conditions in 1995? Starting from the beginning of that year.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, until the beginning of the offensive, that is to say, until mid-July 1995, everything was normal, like in 1994 and the latter half of 1993. There was sufficient food. There was no shelling, except of some sporadic fire, which can be ascribed to the shifts of groups of soldiers which were in certain localities on the hills surrounding Zepa. But immediately before the offensive, perhaps a month before that, the food convoys had been stopped, and after that, the offensive followed. From all sides, from Radava in the north and then Godjenje in the west, and Boksanica to the south, and from the east, from the left bank of Drina, from the area of Rujista, there was non-stop shelling and shooting until the very moment of the fall of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What areas were subject to the shelling that you've described in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: All the populated places were shelled, the entire populated section of Zepa. The only parts that were spared were the facilities where the Ukrainian Battalion was housed and everything else was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular incidents where specific buildings were hit or where people were hurt or killed by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: There was a series of individual incidents when people were killed by shelling. Practically in all the villages, they were killed by shell fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were these people who were killed, to your knowledge, soldiers or were any of them civilians?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mostly civilians inside the town. And practically all of the able-bodied men were on defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did the population try to escape from this shelling?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, you see, most inhabitants had their own shelters which were dug in the ground next to their houses. And if the shelling intensified, people would flee with their children and enter these shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Since we have only talked about shelling in 1995, could you tell us briefly if you recall any incidents of shelling from earlier in the war, 1992 through to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, I said, 1992 was hellish in every sense of the word, especially September 1992. That was the hardest month. And from the direction of Radava, that is to say, from the north of the enclave, and from Laze [phoen] and Borovac to the west, and in the Ribioc sector from the direction of Borika from the south. The same offensive was repeated in May, just before the arrival of UNPROFOR, from the same areas within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said there was an offensive in May just before the arrival of UNPROFOR. Could you tell us which year that was? Again, to be clear for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During those periods of shelling, again the same questions, as I asked in relation to 1995, do you recall if anyone was hurt or killed in any shelling incidents; and, if so, were those soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: At the very beginning of offensive was on Brezova Ravin where an attack was conducted against a facility where a shop was accommodated before the war. Refugees were living there. I'm not sure about the numbers, but I think there were 10 to 12 persons. They all lost their lives. Only one of them had been able-bodied. All the others were women and children. After that, and all-out invasion on Zepa began, and there were people losing their lives in all parts of the territory, and that was caused by shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this incident on Brezova Ravin was that in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, that was the 3rd of May, 1993, in the early hours of the morning. From the direction of Oblaci [phoen], they attacked Brezova Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll move to another subject. During the war, was there any person or persons referred to in Zepa as a hodza?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, there were three such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names, if you remember them, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mehmed Hajric. Ramiz Dumanic. And Jusip Jusipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you know these men personally during the war, or have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I met them during the war. I had not known any of them before the war. All three were refugees. Jusif Jusipovic was not a certified Imam, so to speak. He was still studying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to verify the spelling of these persons' names because what I see in the transcript does not reflect what I heard, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, I think, a fair comment. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you've given us the names of three men. Could you please spell them out, letter by letter, for the names of those three men.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mehmet Hajric, Ramiz Dumanic, Jusif Jusipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the names that have appeared on the screen in front of you showing the transcript, are those the correct spellings for these three mens' names?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mehmet is not spelled like this. It should D. It should end with D, Mehmed. As for Jusif. It should be U instead of I. And the same goes for his last name. Instead of the first I, there should be a U.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think that's clear. Sir, can you tell us about the duties that were performed by these three men during the war?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They were the mosque Imams. They were at the helm of the Dzemat, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you explain briefly what that means? It's not a term that I think we've heard so far in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They were in charge of religious rituals performed in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What do you know about the background of Mr. Hajric before he came to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Not much. I know that he had worked in Podzeplje. His job there was the same as the one he performed in Zepa during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How was the work shared between these three men?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It was probably their internal arrangement as to who would be in charge of what ritual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to each of these men when Zepa fell? Starting, say, with the man you said was not yet qualified as an Imam, Jusuf Jusupovic.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Together with a group of military able-bodied men, Jusuf crossed over to free territory somewhere in or around Kladanj. He had never returned to his Imam studies. He completed his training as a policeman, and he is currently employed as one in Sarajevo where he lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The name is again incorrectly recorded. It is Jusuf Jusupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Jusupovic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So you say that he was --

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- with a group of military able-bodied men and they crossed into free territory. Was this part of the evacuation process or were they travelling on buses or how were they travelling?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No. They were on foot. Different groups organised themselves and each of them looked for their own route in order to reach the free territory controlled by the Army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. So that's Mr. Jusupovic. How about Ramiz Dumanjic? I hope I pronounced his name correctly.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Ramiz Dumanjic was on board of a bus, much like the rest of the population. He was together with his wife and two children. He was in Kakanj immediately following the war. But I wouldn't know where he resides now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know how it was possible for a man with wife and children to leave Zepa on a bus during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: On the first day of evacuation, it was easier to get out. There were less checks, since on that day, the Zepa Brigade commander, Avdo Palic, personally escorted the convoy up to Kladanj. All those who managed to leave on that day, I can freely say, were lucky.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: The witness stated that there were three children. Mr. Dumanjic had three children, not two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, could you clarify that with the witness again please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us again how many children Mr. Dumanjic had when he left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Three children, two daughters and a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, were where you and what were you doing in June and July 1995 before Zepa fell?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: In the second half of June, my wounds became infected. I had sustained them back in 1992. The infection was advanced and there was a lot of puss. I spent a number of days in our outpatient clinic in Zepa and they tried to surgically assist me. Once the offensive began, I returned home in order to make room for those who were more seriously wounded. That's when -- or, actually, it was in that place that I awaited the end of the war or the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you to clarify one sentence. We heard your answer but it was not properly recorded. On page 63, line 25 and the next two lines, the sentence is not complete: "There were less checks, since on that day the Zepa brigade commander, Avdo Palic. Evacuate." I think you should try to clarify this with the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could again tell us how it was possible for Mr. Dumanjic to leave Zepa on the first day of the evacuations. You mentioned Avdo Palic in come context. If you could give that answer again, please, since it is not clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Once the agreement on the evacuation of population was signed with the Serb side, it was arranged that the first convoy was to be escorted by Avdo Palic, in order to indicate to the people how safe it was to embark. The first convoy went through without any problems. No one was mistreated, provoked, or taken off the bus. All following convoys had such events. In other words, people were being taken off buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I believe that's clear on that question now. Sir, can I return to your personal situation. Where were you when you learnt that Zepa had fallen?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: As I said, I was in my family home, that of my parents'.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What day did you learn that Zepa had fallen?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: One day before the evacuation. The first convoy left on Tuesday. And Zepa had fallen on Monday. The first convoy left on Tuesday, which was the 24th, or the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And after you learnt that Zepa had fallen, did you remain at your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, I did not. We went to the mountain that night. From up there, we could see the first convoy leave, and on that same night, we returned to the centre of Zepa, to see how the evacuation process developed, in terms of evacuating the -- those who were wounded, elderly and civilians. I joined those who were wounded, which were split -- who were split in two groups. One group first left on the next day, and I remained as part of the second. We were evacuated on the last day of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb soldiers or officers in Zepa during those days when you were in Zepa town awaiting evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Wednesday and Thursday; that is to say, the last two days of evacuation. That is when I saw General Tolimir, as well as Pecanac, and some people escorting them. They were in that part where the civilians awaited to be evacuated. So there was a small group of soldiers who were with them, perhaps five to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You're giving a bit of detail in a relatively short answer. Just taking your time, tell us about the time or times, when you saw General Tolimir. And you've also mentioned someone called Pecanac, so please also tell us about when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: The wounded, including myself, were placed in front of the old house -- old school building. Those people I mentioned came with Avdo Palic to the area, and this is also where the Ukrainian Battalion was. I don't know whether Dr. Boro came with them or whether he arrived at some later point. He checked all those wounded, made a new list, and that list was actually used during the evacuation. It was on Wednesday, in the morning; that is to say, the second day of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At the time, did you know who Tolimir was?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him personally. I don't know if it was Commander Palic who told us that it was General Tolimir. In any case, I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How about this person Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I think Avdo also told us his name. He was present until the last convoy left Zepa. The last bus of the convoy was where the wounded were, and he helped with that. In other words, he remained until Thursday, the last day of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Again, just because it's not wholly clear from the answer as interpreted in English, you said: "Those people I mentioned came with Avdo Palic to the area." When you say "those people came with Avdo Palic," do you mean the two men we just mentioned, Tolimir and Pecanac, or do you mean some other people?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I had in mind Tolimir, Pecanac and those escorting them. He returned from Kladanj on that day when he saw the convoy off. They came together to the school compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, a correction for the transcript. Your last question, Mr. Elderkin, was: Did you mean Tolimir, Pecanac or others? Pecanac was left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Indeed, I see. And thank you for spotting that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were Tolimir, Pecanac and the other men you saw in the escort doing, if anything, when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They weren't doing anything. They came there with Avdo. They probably had some talks with him, made some plans or arrangements. But I'm not familiar with any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from Avdo Palic, did you see any men from the Bosnian Muslim Army down in Zepa town while you were there waiting to leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: As regards any army members, it was only Avdo Palic who was present there at the time in the centre of Zepa, from where the evacuation process took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know where other members of the army were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They were up in the mountains, to the north of the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, what was the mood among the Muslim population in Zepa during this period when you were down in Zepa town waiting to leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: There was general panic and fear. People worried how things would end. It was a state of total chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At that time, did people know anything about what had happened to the men from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Very little was known. There were only individual cases of people who managed to reach Zepa from Srebrenica. They did tell some things, but, in general terms, people didn't know the actual proportion of what had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at that time, did you personally meet anyone who had come from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I did not. Not at that moment. But once we arrived in the camp, I found Nedzad Kadric from Srebrenica. He retold his story concerning Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us what was that story, as you remember him telling you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. In his words, he managed to crawl out from under the bodies of those who were executed somewhere in the area of Kravica, I believe. He told us that two of his brothers were killed on the occasion, one of whom was his twin brother, and the other one was younger than he was. We didn't go into too much detail as to how and where he had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did he have any injuries himself or did he manage to escape unscathed?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. He had two entry/exit wounds, one on his right leg, and the other in the ribcage area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you and your family feel free to choose whether to stay in Zepa or to leave at the time when the VRS forces had arrived in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, no one even thought of staying because people did not feel safe and were distrustful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, in particular, for military-aged men, were they free to choose to leave in the evacuation, to stay, or to make their own choices?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer that question. Take my word for it when I say that no one even thought about it. The only important thing was to save your hide. No one even pondered staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: To go back very quickly to clear up one point in this account you heard from Nedzad Kadric about him surviving from some kind of execution. Did you learn anything about the numbers of people who had been at that place and who had been subjected to that execution?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I don't recall him mentioning any specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're sticking now to the regular schedule, it looks like it's the break time. And that would be a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it is time for our second break. And we will resume, quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, we finished up just before the break by talking about the atmosphere in Zepa during the evacuation, and we haven't yet covered your own departure from Zepa. So could you tell us how was it that you, as a military-aged man at that time, were waiting to be evacuated from Zepa and were down in Zepa town waiting to leave on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: During the negotiations at Boksanica between the representatives of Zepa and VRS representatives, it was agreed that the civilians and wounded should be evacuated. I fell into the category of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you registered by any international organisation during that period of time, before you left from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it can be qualified as a type of -- a trick. It turned out that we were taken prisoner before we actually were. The ICRC did, indeed, register us within the UN compound in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know on what date they registered you?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: The penultimate day of evacuation. I believe it was the 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people from the ICRC did you see in Zepa at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I'm not certain. Say, four or five people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from registering sick and wounded people, did you see the ICRC staff doing anything else in Zepa, around the time of the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, they didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When did you finally leave Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: On the last day of evacuation, on the 27th, Thursday, sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You told us earlier about seeing Avdo Palic in the company of General Tolimir and Pecanac. Did you see any of those three people again after the time you described before you left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. From the UNPROFOR compound to the bus, we were personally accompanied by Pecanac. Avdo Palic remained as the only inhabitant or member of the Zepa Army within the UN or UNPROFOR compound. In front of the school, a small tent was erected and he stayed there, sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You've referred to the UNPROFOR compound and to the school. Can you clarify whether those are different places or the same place?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It's the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was anyone with Avdo Palic when you saw him outside the compound by this tent?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No. He remained seated alone in the tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said that you were escorted to a bus by Pecanac. Once you got on this bus, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We left Zepa, in the direction of Rogatica. All convoys left in that direction, the ones that had left before ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Who was on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: There were 12 of us who were wounded or sick. The rest were civilians, like women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Once you had left Zepa on the bus, where was the first place that you stopped?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We stopped in the area of Boksanica first, at the check-point of the Ukrainian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How long were you stopped at that check-point?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We stayed until sometime around midnight; that is to say, the whole afternoon until that midnight. Shortly after that, we went on towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During the time the bus was stopped at Boksanica, tell us what was happening. Take as much time as you need. That's a reasonably long period of hours.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Us, the wounded, I think there were some French doctors who took us out and bandaged our wounds in one of their APCs. We didn't know why we stopped there, and I can't recall what time it was exactly. I know that Rajko Kusic, the local commander, entered our bus. I don't know whether he entered any other buses. He introduced himself as Commander Kusic. He asked in a provocative manner where Avdo Palic was. We remained silent. I can even quote what he said. He said, There he is in Zepa shitting his pants. I personally killed him. Sometime before evening, Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric came on the bus. We mentioned him when we discussed the hodzas. They followed the course of the evacuation from Zepa, made up lists, and who was on what bus. They said that it was only to be a brief stop which was to be resolved soon, and then we were supposed to carry on during the night. I don't know why we were stopped at the time. I learned of the reason when I met Mehmet and Amir in the camp. The Serb side sent Mehmet to the mountain to negotiate with the army so that they would hand over their weapons. They were also supposed to surrender. And all those who broke the law and all those who were deemed as being involved in some dirty business were to be prosecuted and the rest would be allowed to leave the area unhindered. If they did not meet that request, they were told that all those who were on the last convoy would be killed. Just before midnight, he returned from the mountain and conveyed the reply of those who were up on the mountain. They categorically refused to surrender. Following that, we resumed our travel to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, sorry for interrupting you. I think on page 73, line 2, an important part of that sentence was not recorded. In relation to Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric. If I recall correctly, the witness said they entered the bus. This was not mentioned. Can you clarify this with the witness again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you began the part of your answer concerning seeing Mr. Hajric and Imamovic by saying something about them, I think, getting on the bus. Could you tell us just in physical terms what happened when you saw them. What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They simply got on the bus. They said that there was an obstacle to be resolved and that we needn't be afraid. They didn't specify what the obstacle or what the cause of the stop was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: As I have said already, I only learned of the reason why we were stopped when I arrived in Rogatica in the camp when I met the two of them. It is only then that they explained the reasons why we were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I believe that clears up the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: -- transcript issue. So if I may continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned Commander Kusic coming onto the bus while you were stopped at Boksanica. While you were at that location, did you see any other Serb soldiers or officers? Did anyone else from the Serb side get on the bus while you were there, apart from Commander Kusic?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They were accompanied by one or two of his escorts. They didn't say anything. As for whether they went on the other buses, that's something I don't know. I didn't discuss it with anyone. No one else entered our buses. Of course, there were other soldiers in the area moving about, but no one approached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You didn't see any generals, anyone higher in rank than Commander Kusic, present at that location?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me refer briefly to a number of your prior statements just to clarify a reference I understand you made to seeing General Mladic at Boksanica. Can you tell me whether you saw General Mladic at that location?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I don't remember I saw him then. I did see him a few times in the camp where he visited while we were down there, but on that day, I do not remember. Perhaps if it is in my statement, it's possible that it was a mistake while it was being typed, but I don't remember seeing him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, I can't now find the reference. I believe I may be mistaken, so I should ask simply to leave that subject and move on. So where did the bus go after leaving Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: After Boksanica, via Rogatica, in the direction of under -- Romanija, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, and in the direction of Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where were you expecting the bus to take you and finally let you leave?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Probably as it had been agreed. We all expected that they would bring us to the free territory; that is to say, territory under the control of the Army of BH, like all other convoys and other civilians who were transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Where did you, in fact, stop in that bus?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: The first time we stopped and took a longer break in the early hours of the morning, perhaps around 5.00 a.m. in Orlovske Luke area. I remember, between a cafe restaurant to the left of the road from Vlasenica to Kladanj which is called Uranak [phoen], so we had been driving not long. I don't know the area very well. I'm not familiar with it. But I heard from the people who were with us that this was Tisca. And there was a school Tisca at the place where we had stopped, and practically it was supposed to be the final destination on our way to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And tell us what happened when the bus had stopped in this location at Tisca?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the bus stopped, an army officer, probably a member of the military police, boarded. He had a white belt and shoulder straps and he boarded the buses and he asked, Are the wounded here? Someone replied that they were. He got off, and to the right of the bus was General Tolimir standing. He gave him a paper of the form at A4 and the officer returned with the very same paper. It was the list of the wounded people. He did a roll-call. There were 12 of us here but he had 13 names on the list, so there was Huso Devedzija, who was missing. He asked what happened to him. No one knew. It was only later that we learned that he left on the previous day with one of the convoys. He order us to get off the bus and move into another one. The other one was parked next to ours, but it was turned into the opposite direction; that is to say, facing Vlasenica. We took our things. We moved there. And perhaps half an hour or 20 minutes after that, they brought another 28 elderly people to the same bus. They were aged between 55 and 60. The bus then started in the direction of Vlasenica; that is to say, the same road we had travelled, all the way to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The 28 elderly people you mentioned being brought onto the second bus that you had been transferred to, do you know where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I was aware from the same convoy by which we had come, and the others had been taken off the buses on the convoy that was travelling the previous night and they spent the night there. They were waiting for us so that we would all return together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said you went all the way to Rogatica. Where did you go in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They first took us to the southern part of the town where the bus station is located. We spent perhaps 15 to 20 minutes there, and then we returned through the town to the northern part, where we were accommodated at the administrative building of the agricultural co-operative called Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Tell us what happened when you first arrived at that location, Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They took us out of the bus, lined us up, they began to search us. They searched through our personal belongings and searched our bodies in the typical way that the police conducts those searches. They perhaps managed to search three or four men, and then General Tolimir came again and told them or ordered them, as you like, to stop that, and let them go inside, into the building. They let us into the biggest room in this building and he also entered it. He said, It is true that we have approved of your evacuation and allowed it, but it was on condition that I believe 48 Serbian prisoners be released at the Dubrava airport near Tuzla. Your side has not honoured this, and we were forced to keep you. Don't worry, this will last two or three days and then it will be resolved. After that, he ordered that the wounded be separated from the elderly persons to a separate room. Once the search was completed, he ordered that a list of all the items that had been taken away be made and that all the belongings should be returned to each person on the day when they are released or exchanged. In any case, he spent a short time there. Then he left, and they continued with their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did Tolimir come on his own or was he with anyone during the time you saw him on your arrival at Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, there was some escort. In addition to him, Milan Mijatovic from Rogatica also came into the room. I know him personally. I'm not sure whether he was a member of the escort or whether he had come there independently. Milan Mijatovic, called Zvijerica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people were brought to the prison camp that day?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Twenty-eight elderly, the 12 wounded, so a total of 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any other prisoners who were already held at this location?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. We found a person from Ilijas, Cuprija [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you visited by the ICRC sometime after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day they visited us, they registered those who had not been registered and their doctors came again on Monday. I think it was Friday when we were brought there, and the doctors came again on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 78, line 20, I think that the witness's answer was not properly translated or not properly recorded. So I would ask the Prosecutor to clarify the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I simply ask the same question again. Sir, could you please tell us about the ICRC visit sometime after you arrived at Rasadnik camp. Indeed, since you can read English and can see perhaps the answer you've given around - at least on my screen - lines 18 through 21 of page 78. And if there's anything to add to that, please, could you add it.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, I can add something to this. On the arrival of the Red Cross, they brought with them and distributed some medical materiel, something for personal hygiene, such as tooth-brushes, brushes, towels for wiping. But there was not sufficient quantity. So we cut them in half so that each prisoner would have one, then some toilet paper. And they also distributed forms which we could sent to our families to inform them of our whereabouts; that is to say, to get in touch with our families through the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the Prosecutor mistaked [as interpreted] the line when he looked at the transcript. Page 78, line 20. I'm -- I had in mind the name of a person and where he is from. I think the witness did not say that he was from Ilijas but that his last name was similar to what is recorded in the transcript. So if we could please clarify this just for the sake of clarity of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I am afraid that we have both LiveNote and ring-tail running on slightly different line numbers. So I apologise for picking out the wrong reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the name of a prisoner you said was from Ilijas. And the name hasn't been picked up correctly in the transcript. Could you please say again his name and, if necessary, spell it.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. It was a person from Visegrad. And his name was Ilijas Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said that General Tolimir addressed the prisoners who arrived in your group and said that you would be in the camp for, I think, two or three days. How long was your group of prisoners, in fact, in this camp?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: We stayed in Rogatica for 172 days, and we waited for the exchange for four days in Kula near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: During this time of your imprisonment, were there any beatings or mistreatment of any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: On the first day, on our arrivals, the beatings started but they took place in the evening when the duty policemen stayed alone without the camp warden and it relatively happened during the night. But the intensity depended on the policemen themselves; that is to say, who of them was on duty. I can even tell you the first and last names of some of them, if needed. Some groups of policemen or pairs of policemen, depending on what their shifts were, had more than decent attitude to all the prisoners and we could literally feel as at home; whereas, there were other groups who were terrible. Intensity of the beatings decreased perhaps after we had spent about ten days there, once we had the work obligation introduced when they started taking the prisoners to work. Probably for the reason that if someone was beaten black and blue, he couldn't work, so then they tried to leave everyone in good physical shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, were all of the prisoners who came to the camp after the fall of Zepa still with you when you left in January of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: All who had been brought there were exchanged in January 1996, expect for Esad Cocalic. He was taken away one evening. I cannot be precise about the date, because this was along time ago. One evening around 10.00 p.m. the room in which is he was accommodated and so was I, Petar Despot, who was the deputy camp warden, came to that room and called on him to come out. He asked, Should I get ready? And the answer was, No, you don't need to. You will go out just for a brief period. He didn't come back that night, and in the morning when we got up to do our everyday duties, each man to his own tasks, the same Petar told us, Esad is happy. He has been exchanged; that is to say, his relative from Libya who was temporarily working in Libya allegedly paid for him, paid a ransom and he was released. Everyone else who had been brought that day was exchanged on the 19th of January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did any other prisoners arrive in the camp during the time you were staying there? People either you saw personally or people you learnt arrived in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: It was like this: Huso Cocalic was brought a day after us. He was exchanged when we were. I cannot be precise whether it was a day or two later, after our arrival. Hamdija Torlak was also brought there. So was Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric. Hamdija was exchanged together with us. As for Amir and Mehmed, I didn't know anything until a year or two ago when their bodies were exhumed in the area of Ragolavi [phoen] near Rogatica. In the meantime, they brought more people to one room, which we called the notorious room. But I cannot be precise. I do not know who was brought there. I can just be precise about the number of people, because we knew how many meals they were taking upstairs, whether those were breakfast, lunches or dinner. This is how we could judge how many people were there. But who exactly was there, and how for long they were kept, this is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you ever learn of a prisoner called Mujo Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes, one of the prisons who were exchanged from the same room told me that. Mujo Hodzic and Mujo Paraganlija, were kept in that room for a while. They were taken away one night, but where, this is something he didn't know, and neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What were the nationalities of those two men, Mujo Hodzic and Mujo Paraganlija?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Tell us what you know about each of them. First of all, Mujo Hodzic, how old was he and where was he from?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I can suppose that he was probably born around 1950, I'm not sure. He could have been a year or two younger or older. And he used to live in the village of Osovo, a dozen kilometres from Rogatica, on the Rogatica-Borike road. He was a refugee throughout the war in Zepa. And as for the circumstances under which he was taken prisoner, and where, I'm not familiar about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How about Mujo Paraganlija?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mujo Paraganlija was younger. He could have been born in 1966 or 1967. He was single, from Zepa or more specifically, from the village of Slap on the banks of the Drina. Once again, I don't know how and where he had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were all the prisoners you encountered, or knew of, Muslims or were there any Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: They were all Muslims. There was not a single Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can you describe the accommodation for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: As General Tolimir ordered them to separate the elderly from the wounded, the elderly men were held in the biggest room in the facility, and I think it was a mess for the labourers from the farm. And we, the wounded, were accommodated in two offices which could have been between 30 to 40 square metres, both of these offices together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you remember the numbers of prisoners who were accommodated in each of the rooms?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: I think that there were seven in one, ten in another, and the others were in the biggest room, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to look at one document, I think, before we finish for the evening, which is Exhibit P1434. Sir, while this is coming up on the screen, this is a VRS document sent, as you'll see from the Rogatica Brigade or 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade Command on the 30th of July, 1995. And I'd ask once it is up on the screen to go, please, to the last page so that we can see the signature block. We can see that it is signed with the following words: "By authorisation from General Tolimir, chief of OBP, Captain Zoran Carkic." I'll start by asking you if you know who was Captain Zoran Carkic?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Yes. Zoran Carkic was the camp warden. Oh, no, Zoran Neskovic was the camp warden. And Zoran Carkic was, I think, in charge of certain duties within the security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska because he visited us and he took statements from us at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did he take any statement from you?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: He didn't take statements from all prisoners and all inmates. He selected several people that he conducted interviews with and took their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Were you one of those people from whom he took a statement, or were you not selected?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: He did not select me and I didn't give him a statement. I gave a statement only to their inspector from the state security, or at least that was how he introduced himself, as an inspector of the state security of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When was that, that you were interviewed by somebody who said they were from state security?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: First week of September. All the prisoners were processed at the time, and they all gave statements to inspectors of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did they ask you about?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mostly about the war activities in the Zepa zone. But the emphasis was on the beginning of the war and Budicin Potok, where a column of their army which was moving in the direction of Zloryrh had been attacked. The rest mainly came down to small scale smuggling and black marketing in the area: Who received goods in Zepa, from whom, how much, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What did they want to know, if you remember, about this attack on the column going towards Zloryrh?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: Mostly who participated in the attack; that is to say, who were the men who had carried out the attack and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could zoom out, please, so that we can stay on the same page but see the paragraph block just above there. Sir, if you can see just above the signature, there's text which talks about a certain Lieutenant Matic and his involvement in searching or robbing some Muslims. Did you ever hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO
utterances.text: The people who were taken off the penultimate convoy and who spent the night in Tisca told us that, on that night, one Matic practically robbed them and took away their money. But I didn't see that, and I cannot confirm it 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I see we're at 7.00, and I have a few more questions on this document. But there's no harm in breaking. I think we can pick it up anyway, because I need to look at the beginning of the document when I start tomorrow, if that suits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we must adjourn for the date. We will resume tomorrow in the morning at 9.00 in this courtroom, number III. The Court Officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
